blocks.text:
This week is taught mainly by Prof. Sivakumar M S ,
with discussions with Prof. Kartic, Lt Col Jayakumar, Prof. Prasanna and
Prof. Shiva. Another name for engineering sense is “thinking
with hands” .

Engineering is as old as
humans

blocks.html:
• Engineering was born from need: to change the environment for food, shelter and security.
  • The driving force: the wish for a better, easier, more comfortable life.
  • Humans invented the wheel, farming, engines, weapons, computers and the internet.
  • Ancient Indian engineers had no degrees, yet they built amazing things. They observed, studied and honed their skills.
blocks.text:
Engineering was born from need : to change the
environment for food, shelter and security . The driving force: the wish for a better, easier, more
comfortable life . Humans invented the wheel , farming , engines , weapons , computers and the internet . Ancient Indian engineers had no degrees , yet they
built amazing things. They observed, studied and honed their
skills .
What went wrong?

blocks.html: The Industrial Revolution (about 200 years ago) brought prosperity, stability and security. But it also made us compartmentalised: everyone is a specialist (heart specialist, foot specialist…). We forget that the whole is more than the sum of its parts.
blocks.text:

blocks.html:
• Today we respect the degree more than real engineering ability.
  • We are great at solving back-of-the-chapter problems, but less ready for real-life problems.

to Chennai? You don’t need a satellite. Put a tub on your terrace,

engineering sense: a quick, smart estimate.
Habit 1: Planning

blocks.html: Planning = arranging what tasks to do, how to do them, and how to use resources well, to reach a goal safely, effectively and efficiently, in the right proportions and within a time limit.
blocks.text:
Planning = arranging what tasks to
do, how to do them, and how to use resources well, to reach a goal safely , effectively and efficiently , in the right proportions and within a time limit .

blocks.html: The word “engineer” comes from the Latin ingenium (cleverness). In old English, an “engine” could also mean a clever plan or plot, so planning sits at the very root of engineering.
blocks.text:
The word “engineer” comes from the Latin ingenium (cleverness). In old English, an “engine” could also
mean a clever plan or plot , so planning sits at the
very root of engineering.

blocks.html:
Lecture example — building a table Even for a simple table, you plan:

  • Materials: wooden planks, legs, nails, paint, in the right quantity.
  • Tools: which tools; do I have them or must I get them?
  • Place: where will I build it?
  • Transport: how will I bring the materials?
blocks.text:
Lecture example — building a table Even for a simple
table, you plan: Materials: wooden planks, legs, nails, paint, in
the right quantity. Tools: which tools; do I have them or must I get
them? Place: where will I build it? Transport: how will I bring the materials?

blocks.caption:
Even a small job needs a plan: materials,
tools, place and transport.

blocks.html:
Lecture example — Prof. Kartic: planning a large IT account When Prof. Kartic took charge of a large account, the first 3–6 months felt like chaos. There were client work, internal teams (delivery excellence, innovation), escalations and staff leaving. His planning steps:

  1. Document everything and spot the patterns of work.
  2. Decide who is best at what.
  3. Give extra roles to small teams, not single “stars”, so work doesn’t stop if one person is away (de-risking).
  4. Set up monitoring: regular meetings to track progress.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — Prof. Kartic: planning a large IT
account When Prof. Kartic took charge of a large account, the
first 3–6 months felt like chaos. There were client work, internal teams
(delivery excellence, innovation), escalations and staff leaving. His
planning steps: Document everything and spot the
patterns of work. Decide who is best at what . Give extra roles to small teams, not single
“stars” , so work doesn’t stop if one person is away
( de-risking ). Set up monitoring : regular meetings to track
progress.

blocks.html: “Your plan may fail, but do not fail to plan.” Keep a plan B and a plan C.
blocks.text:
“Your plan may fail, but do not fail to plan.” Keep
a plan B and a plan C.

blocks.html: Use the right tools: you could turn a screw with a spoon, but a screwdriver is the right tool. Prof. Kartic first built games from scratch, then switched to platforms with ready templates (like crossword templates), which made the work much faster.

Habit 2: Approximating and
estimating

blocks.html: Engineers want a quick ballpark figure: a number that is close enough to be useful.
blocks.text:
Engineers want a quick ballpark figure : a number
that is close enough to be useful.

blocks.html:
Lecture example — the room A cube-shaped room measures 2.05 m on each side.

  • Quick estimate: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 m³.
  • More precise: 2.05 × 2.05 × 2.05 ≈ 8.6 m³. The quick 8 m³ is often good enough to decide things fast. (Note: in the video the lecturer adds only 0.15 and gets 8.15 m³. The correct value is about 8.6 m³.)
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the room A cube-shaped room
measures 2.05 m on each side. Quick estimate: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8
m³ . More precise: 2.05 × 2.05 × 2.05 ≈ 8.6
m³ . The quick 8 m³ is often good enough to decide things fast. (Note: in the video the lecturer adds only 0.15 and gets 8.15 m³.
The correct value is about 8.6 m³.)

blocks.html: Lecture example — the rain in Chennai Put a tub outside during rain. Next day, the water is 3 cm deep. So the rainfall was about 3 cm. Water received ≈ 3 cm × area of Chennai. That gives a useful estimate.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the rain in Chennai Put a tub
outside during rain. Next day, the water is 3 cm deep.
So the rainfall was about 3 cm. Water received ≈ 3 cm × area of
Chennai. That gives a useful estimate.

blocks.caption:
Measure a little, multiply by the big
area, and you have a good estimate.

blocks.html: Another example: after demonetisation, a friend asked how many rupees change hands in India each day. Look at one part of a city, then extrapolate.
blocks.text:

Habit 3: Technical
auditing: “What is conserved?”

blocks.html: Technical auditing means checking what should balance, and asking where the difference went. It is based on conservation: some quantities (energy, mass, money, people) can’t just disappear.
blocks.text:
Technical auditing means checking what should balance, and asking where the difference went.
It is based on conservation : some quantities (energy,
mass, money, people) can’t just disappear.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the bouncing ball Drop a ball from 2 m. It bounces back lower. Energy is conserved, so where did the rest go? It became heat, sound and friction at impact.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the bouncing ball Drop a ball from
2 m. It bounces back lower . Energy is conserved, so where did the rest go? It became heat , sound and friction at impact.

blocks.caption:
The ball doesn’t come back as
high. The “missing” energy went into heat and sound.

blocks.html: Lecture example — cement + sand 1 bag of cement + 1 bag of sand ≠ 2 bags of mix. Some cement fills the gaps between sand grains, so the volume is less. But the weight is the same, because weight is what’s conserved.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — cement + sand 1 bag of cement + 1
bag of sand ≠ 2 bags of mix. Some cement fills the gaps between sand grains, so the volume is less. But the weight is the same, because weight is what’s
conserved .

blocks.html: Lecture example — hostel rooms and mess food As Dean, Prof. Sivakumar used auditing for hostel occupancy: the number of rooms is fixed, so the count must balance. With Lt Col Jayakumar, he audited mess food waste: how much was cooked, served, eaten and wasted. Plate waste went to a biogas plant; unserved food went to NGOs.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — hostel rooms and mess food As
Dean, Prof. Sivakumar used auditing for hostel occupancy: the number of
rooms is fixed, so the count must balance. With Lt Col Jayakumar, he
audited mess food waste : how much was cooked, served,
eaten and wasted. Plate waste went to a biogas plant ;
unserved food went to NGOs .

blocks.html: Lecture example — army operations (Lt Col Jayakumar) Every day is an audit. For road opening and convoy protection, the cook has tea ready at 4 a.m., the armoury opens, weapons are checked, vehicles are ready by 5:15, and the road is declared clear by 7 a.m. For an attack “by 0500 hours”, the commander works backwards: resources (own and borrowed), who does what, transport and fuel, ammunition (and when reserves may be used), time, and environment (moonlight, rain). Afterwards: count the people and the stores. Training + maintenance + inventory control keep a unit “fit for war at all times”.

sections.title: Apply What You Learn, Find the Cause, Make It Better

blocks.html: Start here A plastic sheet is very hard to tear. Make one tiny cut with scissors, and it tears easily along that line. Now, where else could you use this trick? Notebooks with perforated pages! That question, “where else can I use this?”, is an engineer’s habit.

Habit 5:
Relate cause to effect (root cause analysis)

blocks.html: Find the root cause. Then you can control the effect.
blocks.text: Find the root cause . Then you can control the effect .

blocks.html: Lecture example — putting out a fire Fire needs oxygen (cause → burning). Throw a blanket over a small fire, and the little oxygen under it is used up, so the fire goes out. Knowing the cause tells you how to stop the effect.
blocks.text:
Lecture example — putting out a fire Fire needs oxygen (cause → burning). Throw a blanket over a small fire, and the little oxygen under
it is used up, so the fire goes out. Knowing the cause tells you how to
stop the effect.

Habit 6: How can I make it
better?

blocks.html: Humans are never satisfied with the first version. The question “How can I make it better?” drives every improvement.
blocks.text:
Humans are never satisfied with the first version.
The question “How can I make it better?” drives every
improvement.

blocks.caption:
Each version solved a
problem of the one before.

blocks.html: Lecture example — the computer mouse Bulky first mouse → rolling-ball mouse (but the ball got stuck and depended on the surface) → optical mouse → ergonomic mouse → gestures. Each step began by asking: where is the problem, and how can I fix it?
blocks.text:
Lecture example — the computer mouse Bulky first
mouse → rolling-ball mouse (but the ball got stuck and
depended on the surface) → optical mouse → ergonomic mouse → gestures . Each step
began by asking: where is the problem, and how can I fix it?

blocks.html:
Lecture example — railway ticket booking (Prof. Kartic)

  1. 1980s: only 1–2 big booking halls in a city (like Chennai Central and Egmore), many long queues, tickets written by hand in ledgers. Half a day lost.
  2. Booking offices opened in different parts of the city, saving travel time.
  3. Chairs for waiting passengers, a kind thought (empathy) for senior citizens.
  4. One single queue feeding all counters, so nobody has to guess which queue is faster.
  5. Online booking, plus licensed agents for people who aren’t tech-savvy, which also cut down corruption.
  6. Mobile app and SMS tickets: no paper, which is also good for the environment.

Teachers kept asking, “Can I use this for a test?” So, out of empathy, he chose platforms that also show analytics (who played, scores, difficulty of each question), while keeping the fun.

Habit 7: Change your
perspective

blocks.html: A solution rejected in the past may become the best one when the situation changes.
blocks.text:
A solution rejected in the past may become the best
one when the situation changes.

blocks.html: Lecture example — DC power is back Edison’s DC power couldn’t travel far because too much was lost in the cables. Tesla’s AC could, so AC won. Today, solar panels produce DC power locally, close to where it is used. So DC systems are worth looking at again. (IIT Madras works on such DC electrification projects.) Lesson: Don’t throw away old solutions. Re-check them from today’s perspective.

sections.title: Big Picture, Abstraction, and Divide and Conquer

blocks.html: Start here You need to drive a nail into a wall but have no hammer. Most people give up. An engineer asks, “What does a hammer actually do?” It creates an impact. Now a stone, a heavy book or a shoe heel can all do the job.
blocks.text:

have no hammer. Most people give up. An engineer asks, “What does a
hammer actually do ?” It creates an impact . Now a stone, a heavy book or a shoe heel can
all do the job.
Habit 8: Big-picture thinking

blocks.html: You met this in systems thinking. Look at the bird’s-eye view, then come back to the details, and go back and forth between them.
blocks.text:
You met this in systems thinking. Look at the bird’s-eye
view , then come back to the details , and go
back and forth between them.

blocks.html:
Type Question
Spatial (space) What does the whole situation look like from above?
Temporal (time) What has happened, or will happen, over time?
blocks.text: Type Question Spatial (space) What does the whole situation look like from above? Temporal (time) What has happened, or will happen, over time?

blocks.html: Lecture example — four years at IIT (Prof. Shiva) On day 1, a new student misses home and hates the food. From the “helicopter”, he can see his whole four years: graduating and receiving his degree on stage. The small daily troubles become easier to bear. The helicopter also shows the bad future (failing, falling behind), so he can correct course now by studying regularly.

Habit 9: Abstraction and
detailing

blocks.caption:
Ask “why?” to go up
to the principle. Ask “how?” to come down to a real tool.

blocks.html:
Move Question to ask Hammer example
Abstraction (go up to the principle) **“Why** does it work?” A hammer is really an impact (impulse) generator
Detailing (come down to a real thing) **“How** can I create an impact?” A hammer, a stone, a heavy book…
blocks.text:
Move Question to ask Hammer example Abstraction (go up to the principle) **“Why** does it work?” A hammer is really an impact (impulse)
generator Detailing (come down to a real thing) **“How** can I create an impact?” A hammer, a stone, a heavy book…

blocks.html: Why it helps (Prof. Shiva):
blocks.text: Why it helps (Prof. Shiva):

blocks.html:
• “What is an alternative to a hammer?” limits your thinking. “What else can cause an impact?” opens it up.
  • It builds confidence. Instead of “I don’t have a hammer, I’m stuck”, you think “What else can do the job?”
  • In life: people often get depressed because they lack one specific thing. Abstraction shows them other ways to reach the same goal.

Habit 10: Divide and conquer

blocks.html: Break a big system or problem into smaller functions and sub-functions, solve each, and keep track of how they connect.
blocks.text:

Breaking big
goals into tiny steps (Prof. Prasanna)

blocks.alt: Tiny steps to a big goal
blocks.caption:
A big goal becomes doable when you
break it into small steps.

blocks.html:
• “A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.”
  • To climb Everest, know the goal, then plan small steps.
  • Small steps mean less stress: you can see your progress.
  • Mistakes are small, so course correction is easy.
  • Methods like Kaizen, Lean and Six Sigma all work by breaking big processes into small steps.
  • 1% better each day → about 37 times better in a year (1.01³⁶⁵ ≈ 37.8).
  • An engineer building a house: foundation first, then one floor at a time, and finally a beautiful building.

Levers in life (Prof. Shiva)

blocks.caption:
A smile, a kind word or a
well-timed question can be a lever.

blocks.html: “Give me a lever long enough and I can move the world.” — often credited to Archimedes
blocks.text:
“Give me a lever long enough and I can move the world.” — often
credited to Archimedes

blocks.html: Levers are everywhere, if you look for them:
blocks.text: Levers are everywhere, if you look for them:

blocks.html:
• In court (“courtcraft”): the judge’s mood, the time of day, a smile, a friendly word to the opposing lawyer before the hearing.
  • At home: your son comes home late. Instead of getting angry, use the relationship as a lever and talk calmly.
  • In coaching: a sudden bang on the table or a change in voice tone is a cue to explore the feeling behind it.
  • A smile, a pat on the back and appreciation are all levers.

blocks.html: Start here In 1947, Indian troops were rushed to defend Kashmir. They found a battery of guns ready to fire, but the gun sights had all been sent away for overhaul. Nobody had checked. A simple “before” and “after” audit could have saved precious time.

Exchange ideas,
collaborate, and debrief
Communities of practice

blocks.html: Lt Col Jayakumar: in the army, soldiers on the ground log information in real time. Commanders review it weekly or monthly, discuss options (war gaming), and decide where to put effort. Information flows down to the last soldier, and feedback flows back up.

Mental models

blocks.html: We take in the world through our senses and build a simplified picture of it in our minds. Prof. Sivakumar calls this the “cartoonery of the mind”.

blocks.html:
Prof. Prasanna’s points
Like local storage of web pages Saved in our own way for quick use
They help us Focus, connect the dots faster, make decisions, forecast
But they can block new thinking An old model can stop you from seeing new options
So deconstruct and rebuild them often Throw out what no longer works; keep the mind uncluttered

Changing perspectives

blocks.html:
Lecture example — Prof. Prasanna’s career

  • First job: about money, a good company, a good location. Living alone as a paying guest (cooking, shopping, accounts) gave her a new respect for her parents.
  • Second job: she protected time for herself. Travel around the world broke many mental models.
  • She once thought, “I only work well when someone tells me what to do.” Later she wanted purpose and impact, quit her regular job, and became a life coach: “jumping off a cliff”. Perspectives keep changing, and that’s how we grow.

Thinking
like a lawyer and an engineer (Prof. Shiva)

blocks.html:
Skill Meaning Lecture example
Deconstruction Dig into what actually happened A landlord said the tenant hadn’t paid rent for 5 months. Cross-examination showed the tenant had asked for the bank details many times. The judge saw the intention to pay, and the tenant stayed.
Deduction Reach a firm conclusion from facts A witness says he saw a man on a road at night. The calendar shows it was a new-moon night, too dark to see. So the claim is false.
Induction Reach a likely conclusion from signs “The clouds are dark, so it may rain.”

blocks.text: What is engineering sense?

blocks.html:
• Thinking with hands. Engineering was born from the need for food, shelter and security.

  • The Industrial Revolution made us narrow specialists. Don’t forget the whole.
  • Engineering is a habit.
